ZSPC is relevant to VR/simulation but is a micro-cap speculative exception with budget and liquidity risk; it should not be ranked alongside preferred $300M-$10B candidates without stronger customer and financial evidence.

Clinical-placement management looks like the most actionable scarce supplier sub-node; simulation labs and VR are relevant but public pure-play exposure is less clean.

APEI is a small-cap underfollowed nursing-capacity candidate through Rasmussen University and Hondros College of Nursing; verify market cap, NCLEX outcomes, clinical-placement constraints, regulatory risk, and segment profitability before advancing.

HSTM is a second-order software/credentialing infrastructure hypothesis rather than a proven university nursing-program supplier; needs customer-level evidence linking products to academic healthcare training or clinical-placement workflows.

Healthcare licensure education capacity appears to be constrained by physical labs, simulation/VR investment, clinical placements, faculty, accreditation, and state licensure pathways, not only by online-course content.

Need a separate supplier pass for simulation equipment and VR: CAE Healthcare, Laerdal, Gaumard, UbiSim/Labster, Elsevier/HESI, ATI/Ascend, Exxat/InPlace clinical-placement software, and private vendors may define the true chokepoint even when public-market exposure is indirect.
ATGE should remain the reference leader for public healthcare/nursing licensure education exposure, especially Chamberlain nursing and employer-linked clinical-readiness pathways.

The healthcare licensure capacity node appears to span operators, university service providers and healthcare workforce software; strongest chokepoint tests are simulation lab availability, clinical placement access, faculty supply, state authorization, accreditation and NCLEX outcomes.

Public pure-play nursing simulation hardware, VR clinical training and clinical-placement vendors appear limited; many likely suppliers are private, embedded in universities, or too small, so later searches should verify whether any US-listed micro/small-cap exceptions exist.

summary: Combined focused Layer 1B searches: Layer 1B expansion finds two direct education asset/service owners with high exposure to healthcare licensure capacity, one niche healthcare workforce software supplier, and one micro-cap speculative AR/VR simulation supplier. The strongest direct fits are LOPE and ATGE because their disclosed businesses explicitly include ABSN, OTA, nursing, healthcare programs, campuses, online delivery, simulation labs, or partner operations. HSTM is a second-order supplier to healthcare organizations, nursing schools, and nursing students. ZSPC is a speculative shadow candidate because it has direct AR/VR healthcare-training evidence but is far below the preferred market-cap range and depends heavily on education budgets. Layer 1B expansion found a small universe of US-listed names tied to healthcare-licensure education capacity, with the strongest underfollowed chokepoint signal in clinical-placement software and healthcare workforce-learning infrastructure. HealthStream appears to be the cleanest small-cap supplier candidate after acquiring clinical-rotation management assets in 2024. Grand Canyon Education is a mid-cap program-services operator with explicit ABSN/OTA, simulation, VR, and prerequisite-strategy exposure through university partners. Adtalem is a reference capacity operator because Chamberlain is a large nursing-school platform with clinical hub expansion, but it is less of a hidden supplier.
